name: split-panel

split.note: Read-across (asymmetric): an overflowing feature+points panel is re-authored as a feature cover followed by the supporting points flowed onto clean pages, rather than clipped. lib/core/carousel.js.

density.note: one finding per row, a sentence

description: Featured left panel + supporting right zone — one prominent claim beside the points that substantiate it.
purpose: Use when one prominent element (a heading, a hero number, a pull-quote, a phase) deserves a dedicated panel and the right side carries the supporting points. The default anchors a heading; variants reshape what the panel features: `metric` (hero number, light-left), `pullquote` (pull-quote), `steps` (numbered step-timeline), `watermark` (accent panel + letterform + meta footer). For a binary decision with a verdict, reach for `split-compare`.

eyebrow.description: Optional inline-code label above the feature (the phase number under `steps`, the unit under `metric`).

heading.description: The featured element in the left panel — a heading by default; a hero number under `metric`; the phase name under `steps`. (Under `pullquote`, use a blockquote instead — see the variant.)

lede.description: One-sentence framing paragraph under the feature.

points.description: Right-side supporting points. Each li's lead is the point title — it renders bold automatically (no `**…**`); follow it with a nested `- body` line.

`Eyebrow context`

## Headline that anchors the panel.

One-sentence framing paragraph explaining what the points cover.

- First point
  - Supporting detail explaining the first point.
- Second point
  - Supporting detail explaining the second point.
- Third point
  - Supporting detail explaining the third point.
sample:
<!-- _class: split-panel -->

`statement · split-panel`

## The featured panel makes the claim; this side supports it.

A dark left panel carries the headline, and the bright right column holds up to three supporting items.

- Two zones, one argument
  - The split is hierarchy, not decoration — the panel claims, the column proves.
- Three items is the comfort zone
  - A short title and one supporting line each, like this.
- Prose stays on a budget
  - Sixteen words per item keeps the column scannable.

whenToUse.title: One feature, supporting points
whenToUse.body: When a single prominent element — a thesis heading, a hero number, a quote — deserves its own panel and the right side substantiates it. The panel is the anchor; the right is the evidence.

whenToUse.title: Pick the variant by what the panel features
whenToUse.body: Heading (default), hero number (`metric`), pull-quote (`pullquote`), phase + numbered steps (`steps`), or an accent panel with a letterform watermark and a metadata footer (`watermark`).

whenToUse.title: Points carry a title + body
whenToUse.body: Each right-side item leads with a bold title (lifted automatically) and a nested one-line body. Three or four points read best; more crowds the panel.

antiPatterns.title: A binary decision with a verdict
antiPatterns.body: If the slide weighs two options and lands a recommendation, use `split-compare` — its right zone is a 2-option grid + a verdict card, which `split-panel` does not provide.

antiPatterns.title: Co-equal halves
antiPatterns.body: split-panel is asymmetric — a featured panel beside supporting detail. For two co-equal options side by side, use `compare-prose`.

antiPatterns.title: A list with no feature
antiPatterns.body: If there's no prominent left-panel element, a plain `list` or `cards-stack` serves better — the panel earns its place only when one element leads.

steps.label: steps
steps.caption: The panel anchors a numbered phase.
steps.sample:
<!-- _class: split-panel steps -->

`02`

## steps

The left panel anchors a phase; the column numbers its moves.

1. Watermark the phase
   - The inline-code number becomes the panel's backdrop.
2. Number the column
   - An ordered list reads as sequence — three steps fit.
3. Keep steps parallel
   - Verb-first titles, one supporting line each.

## Watermark

### The heading's first letter becomes the panel

- The accent panel decorates
  - A large letterform behind the heading — presence without a photo.
- The h3 subtitles
  - One line naming what the slide surveys.
- The column carries the content
  - Same three-item budget as the default split.

mirror.caption: Featured panel moves right.

`split-panel mirror`

## mirror puts the featured panel on the right.

Same anatomy, flipped — for when the deck's rhythm wants the claim to land late.

- Reading order still works
  - The eye crosses support first, then lands on the panel's claim.
- Use it sparingly
  - One mirror per section keeps the flip meaningful.

stressDoc.caption: Three items at full budget.
stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: split-panel -->

`split-panel · stress`

## Three full items is this column's ceiling.

The framing paragraph can run two lines when every item below uses its whole budget, but nothing here may run longer.

- First item at full width
  - Sixteen words of support is the budget, and this line is written to land exactly on it, deliberately.
- Second item, same weight
  - Parallel structure keeps a maxed column readable; vary the openings and the scan collapses.
- Third item closes the set
  - A fourth would push past the footer — split the slide instead.
